meta.subtitle: Integrated energy major; prices, refining margins and Hess volumes drove a strong Q2'26, but consensus EPS steps down in FY27 and the shares sit near their high

advisories: model vs Street expected return diverge by 59pp — informational, not scored

analystSentiment.commentary: Chevron's second quarter of 2026 was strong. Net income attributable to Chevron rose to $12.1 billion ($6.11 per diluted share) from $2.5 billion ($1.45) a year earlier. The company credits higher commodity prices, higher margins on refined product sales and higher sales volumes; production rose 20 percent with the Hess assets, and Brent averaged $104 per barrel against $68. The quarter also brought an $8.4 billion cut in total debt, after total debt had risen to $40.8 billion at FY25 year-end. The difficulty is the price. At $204.88 the shares sit near the top of their $146.49–$217.78 52-week range, and consensus expects EPS to step down from $16.19 in FY26E to $13.57 in FY27E. Our scenarios apply today's 15.1x year-ahead multiple throughout, so the Base equals the price by construction. The call comes from a Bear downside deeper than the Bull upside, which weights to a fair value of $200.50, slightly below the price, with a Bear case at $147. We rate the shares HOLD with a $182–$225 target range. The valuation section tests every anchor on the page against that call.

executiveSummary.companyOverview: Chevron Corporation is an integrated energy and chemicals company with two businesses. Upstream explores for, develops, produces and transports crude oil and natural gas; processes, liquefies and regasifies liquefied natural gas; and operates carbon capture and storage and a gas-to-liquids plant. Downstream refines crude oil into petroleum products; markets crude oil, refined products and lubricants; makes renewable fuels; and manufactures commodity petrochemicals, plastics for industrial uses, and fuel and lubricant additives. The company lists substantial activities in countries from Angola and Argentina to Kazakhstan, Guyana, the United States and Venezuela. Incorporated in Delaware in 1926 as Standard Oil Company of California, it adopted the Chevron name in 1984, became ChevronTexaco in 2001 and returned to Chevron Corporation in 2005; it is headquartered in Houston, Texas. In July 2025 it completed its acquisition of Hess Corporation, whose legacy assets the company credits for much of the recent production growth. The data pack shows revenue as one consolidated line, $189.0 billion in FY25, while the 10-Q reports earnings for the Upstream and Downstream segments; we follow the filing's segment view for earnings and quote no segment revenue split.

thesis.label: HOLD
thesis.body: Chevron is executing well, but at $204.88 much of a favorable commodity backdrop is already in the price. The Q2'26 result rested on higher commodity prices, higher margins on refined product sales and higher volumes from Hess and U.S. production, and management delivered its Hess synergy and structural cost targets early. Against that, consensus sees EPS falling from FY26E to FY27E, and the shares have climbed from the low end of their 52-week range to near the top. Holding today's year-ahead multiple gives a Base close to the current price and a probability-weighted value slightly below it, so the call is HOLD. The 3.52% dividend yield pays holders to wait; it does not create a margin of safety.

catalysts: Hess synergies: $1.5 billion of annual run-rate synergies within a year of the July 2025 close, 50 percent above the initial target.
Cost program: $3 billion of annual run-rate structural savings captured six months early, against a $3-4 billion target for the end of 2026.
Data-center power: a 20-year power purchase agreement to supply about 2.67 gigawatts of behind-the-meter capacity to a Microsoft data center in West Texas.
Debt paydown: the July 31, 2026 release reports total debt reduced by $8.4 billion in Q2'26.
Portfolio: the Hong Kong fuels and lubricants sale closed in Q2'26, and the sale of the Singapore Refining Company stake is expected to close in 2027.
risks: Commodity prices: upstream earnings follow crude, natural gas and NGL prices set in global markets, and the latest quarter had unusually high prices behind it.
Earnings step-down: consensus EPS falls from FY26E to FY27E, and the valuation section weighs the risk of a further decline.
Entry price: the shares trade near their 52-week high after a large rise from the low.
Middle East conflict: it curtailed Partitioned Zone production and cut international refinery throughput in Q2'26.
Balance sheet: total debt rose sharply in FY25, and capital returns that year exceeded free cash flow.

income.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended December 31.

financials.incomeCommentary: Revenue follows the commodity cycle. It rose {+ +51.6% +} to $246.3 billion in FY22, fell {- -18.4% -} to $200.9 billion in FY23, was little changed at $202.8 billion in FY24 and fell {- -6.8% -} to $189.0 billion in FY25. Net income moved further than revenue, from $35.5 billion in FY22 to $12.3 billion in FY25, and diluted EPS from $18.28 to $6.63. Gross margin stayed between 40.7% and 43.2% across the five years and ended FY25 at 42.8%; on a trailing-twelve-month basis the gross margin is 45.4% and the net margin 9.6%. The interim results mark a turn. Q2'26 revenue was $70.1 billion, {+ up 56.3% +} year over year, and net income attributable to Chevron was $12.1 billion ($6.11 per diluted share) against $2.5 billion ($1.45) in Q2'25. Upstream earned $8.2 billion against $2.7 billion, which the company attributes mainly to higher realizations and higher sales volumes, partly offset by higher depreciation, depletion and amortization. Downstream earned $4.9 billion against $737 million on higher margins on refined product sales, and All Other was a $978 million net charge. Timing effects swing the quarters: the MD&A reports $1.5 billion of favorable timing effects in Q2'26 after a $2.9 billion adverse effect in Q1'26, while the release's highlights give $1.4 billion for Q2; we use the MD&A figure. Adjusted earnings, which exclude items including a $230 million asset-sale gain and $86 million of pension settlement costs, were $12.0 billion ($6.06 per diluted share). Consensus revenue is $229.6 billion for FY26E and $213.8 billion for FY27E, so the Street expects the top line to fall back after this year.

balance.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended December 31.

financials.balanceCommentary: Leverage rose in FY25 and has started to come down. Total debt fell from $31.4 billion in FY21 to $20.8 billion in FY23, then rose to $24.5 billion in FY24 and $40.8 billion in FY25, the year Chevron completed the Hess acquisition; the pack does not show how much of the increase came with the deal. Net debt followed the same path. It was lowest at $5.7 billion in FY22, when cash and short-term investments reached $17.9 billion, and stood at $33.5 billion at FY25 year-end, with cash of $7.3 billion. Chevron carried net debt, not net cash, in every year of the series. The second quarter reversed part of the rise: the July 31, 2026 release reports that total debt was reduced by $8.4 billion in Q2'26 and gives net debt-to-CFFO of 0.6x and debt-to-CFFO of 0.8x for the quarter, against 1.3x and 1.5x in Q1'26, the prior quarter. The pack carries no EBITDA-based leverage or interest coverage, so those company ratios are the best current read. Total equity rose to $192.2 billion in FY25 from $153.2 billion in FY24, and liquidity is adequate, with a current ratio of 1.15 at FY25 year-end and 1.25 on a trailing basis. On balance, leverage is moderate rather than low: the FY25 increase was large, and the quarterly paydown shows debt falling while prices are high. The test comes if prices fall before more of the FY25 increase is repaid.

cashflow.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended December 31.

financials.cashflowCommentary: Operating cash flow has held up across the cycle: $49.6 billion in FY22, $35.6 billion in FY23, $31.5 billion in FY24 and $33.9 billion in FY25. Capital expenditure more than doubled over the five years, from $8.1 billion in FY21 to $17.3 billion in FY25, so free cash flow fell from its $37.6 billion peak in FY22 to $16.6 billion in FY25, an 8.8% FCF margin; the trailing FCF yield is 6.7%. Capital returns ran ahead of that: FY25 dividends paid were $12.8 billion and share repurchases only slightly less, together exceeding free cash flow, in a year when total debt rose and cash fell. The pack does not show what funded the gap, so we do not tie the debt increase to the returns. The interim figures are stronger. The release reports cash flow from operations of $22.6 billion in Q2'26 against $8.6 billion a year earlier, which it attributes to U.S. production with higher commodity prices, increased cash distributions from Tengizchevroil LLP and favorable working capital effects. For the six months, cash flow from operations was $25.1 billion against $13.8 billion. Free cash flow was $18.1 billion for the quarter. In the second quarter cash generation was enough to cut debt sharply; at FY25's level it did not cover returns, so returns at the recent pace depend on prices staying firm.

multiples.note: Peer multiples pending a peer data source.

valuation.multiplesCommentary: On trailing-twelve-month earnings, which include quarters well below the latest one, Chevron trades at 19.7x, and at 8.7x trailing EV/EBITDA and 1.9x sales. The forward multiples need one basis. The vendor's 12.7x NTM P/E is close to the price over FY26E EPS of $16.19, so it reads as a current-year multiple on a strong year. The price over FY27E EPS of $13.57 is 15.1x, the multiple on next year's earnings. The gap between the two reflects the earnings step-down consensus expects, not a difference in how the market rates the business. Our scenarios use that year-ahead multiple throughout, applied a year from now to each scenario's year-ahead EPS, so every price rests on the same basis. The Street is constructive: 25 analysts split 20 Buy, 4 Hold and 1 Sell, with a consensus target of $222.17 (+8.4%), a median of $224.50 and a range of $175.00–$245.00. We do not adopt the consensus target as our Base, because the pack gives no multiple or EPS behind it that we can check against the scenarios.

scenarios.name: Bull
scenarios.driver: Brent stays near the $92 first-half 2026 average, so earnings near FY26E EPS of $16.19 prove repeatable rather than a peak. At today's 15.1x year-ahead multiple that gives about $245, the top of the Street target range.

scenarios.name: Base
scenarios.driver: Consensus holds: EPS steps down to FY27E's $13.57 and stays near that level a year later, which on our reading needs Brent between the Bear's and the Bull's levels, nearer the Bull's. At the same year-ahead multiple that gives $205, today's price by construction; the scenario commentary tests other anchors.

scenarios.name: Bear
scenarios.driver: Brent falls back toward the $68 of Q2'25 and earnings revert to around FY24's $9.72 EPS, above FY25's $6.63 because full-year Hess volumes and the cost savings cushion the fall. At the same year-ahead multiple that gives $147, about the $146.49 52-week low.

valuation.scenarioCommentary: We weight Bull 25%, Base 50% and Bear 25%, for a fair value of $200.50 against the $204.88 price. The Base applies today's price over FY27E EPS to that same EPS, so it equals the price by construction; the label comes from the Bear's larger downside against the Bull's upside and from the weights. In oil terms, flat earnings after FY27 need Brent between the Bear's $68 and the Bull's $92, nearer the upper end on our reading, held for a year. For that: FY27E already prices a step down from FY26E, so the Base needs prices to stop falling rather than stay at second-quarter levels, and continued volume growth in the Permian Basin and Gulf of America could absorb a modest further decline. Against it: the MD&A says commodity prices declined in June 2026, and FY27E EPS is still above every year from FY23 to FY25. We use one year-ahead multiple in all three scenarios. In the Bull, earnings near FY26E prove repeatable, which removes the step-down that the 12.7x on FY26E discounts today; the Bull lands on the top of the Street target range and the Bear on about the $146.49 52-week low, two checks a reader can verify. The counter-reading is that the market pays only that lower multiple on FY26E-level earnings today; at it the Bull, or a Base at the same current-year multiple on FY27E, derives SELL. In the other direction, the higher trailing multiple shows the market paying more for lower earnings, so the Bear could hold a higher multiple than we give it, which would lift the fair value but keep HOLD. The one price-independent anchor, the consensus target, keeps HOLD if used as the Base, as does a Base at the Street high. Every anchor on the page derives HOLD or SELL, and none derives BUY. Moving five points of weight from Bull to Bear keeps HOLD; ten points derives SELL. The call is close to SELL and rests on judgment. Refining margins and timing effects, which helped Q2'26, are not modelled separately but sit inside each scenario's EPS. The Bear is not deepened for net debt, which a P/E-based price already reflects. The $182–$225 range brackets the $205 Base.

segments.name: Consolidated
segments.body: Chevron runs and reports two businesses, as the overview notes. Upstream is the larger earnings source and the company states that its results depend mostly on that segment, whose main driver is the crude price set in global markets. Its scale grew with Hess: net oil-equivalent production was 4,070 MBOED in Q2'26 against 3,396 MBOED a year earlier, and U.S. output of 2,077 MBOED was up 382,000 barrels per day year over year on Hess and growth in the Permian Basin and Gulf of America. Downstream turns crude, its main cost, into refined products and chemicals; U.S. refinery crude unit throughput was 1.07 million barrels per day at more than 97 percent utilization. The integration gives a partial hedge, because refining margins can hold up when crude eases, but it does not offset a broad price decline, since upstream carries most of the earnings.

moatFactors.name: Cost position
moatFactors.body: Long-lived resources in the Permian Basin, the Gulf of America and the legacy Hess assets, plus the structural savings, lower the price Chevron needs to cover its costs. Return on capital employed was 21.4% in Q2'26 against 6.2% a year earlier, which shows how much of that return comes from price. In a price-taking business a cost edge lowers the breakeven; it does not set the price.

moatFactors.name: Scale and integration
moatFactors.body: Operating both Upstream and Downstream across many countries spreads operating and political risk and funds capital-intensive projects that run for decades. Downstream earnings rose with refined-product margins in Q2'26, a partial offset to crude exposure rather than a hedge against a broad downturn.

moatFactors.name: Financial capacity
moatFactors.body: Cash-flow-based leverage is low on the latest quarter's strong cash flow but moderate on the FY25 balance sheet, as set out in the financials. That capacity supports investment and the dividend through a downturn, but the FY25 debt increase makes it a moderate rather than a strong advantage until more of it is repaid.

businessMoat.durability: The moat is narrow, not wide, because Chevron sells commodities whose prices it does not control. Its risk factors state that the prices of crude oil, natural gas and NGLs are the most significant factor in its results, and the fall in net income from FY22 to FY25 shows how cyclical the business is. What lasts is the cost position, the scale and the financial capacity to invest through the cycle. The longer-term question is the energy transition: the company says policy, technology and consumer-preference shifts could change demand for its products, while noting that many published outlooks conclude fossil fuels will remain a significant part of the energy system for many years. The position is defensible over a normal commodity cycle and exposed to a structural demand shift over decades.

points: Production is the lever Chevron controls most. Q2'26 output rose 20 percent year over year on Hess and growth in the Permian Basin and Gulf of America, and higher volumes were one of the two main reasons upstream earnings rose. The offsets are real: higher depreciation, depletion and amortization absorbed part of the gain, and international output was curtailed in the Partitioned Zone. Volume growth supports earnings at a given price, which is the core of our Base case.

Hess synergies reached $1.5 billion of annual run-rate within a year of the July 2025 close, 50 percent above the initial target. With the target already beaten, the remaining question is whether legacy Hess barrels keep contributing at this quarter's pace; the synergy upside itself looks largely captured.

Structural cost reductions of $3 billion a year were captured six months early, against a $3-4 billion target by the end of 2026, measured against 2024 levels. Lower structural cost reduces the oil price at which Chevron covers its dividend and capital program, which is our own reading; the 2026 proxy lists lowering the Brent breakeven price into the next decade among management's objectives. The rest of that range is the incremental upside from here, and it is modest relative to the earnings swing from price.

Chevron signed a 20-year power purchase agreement with Microsoft and agreed to develop a West Texas facility providing about 2.67 gigawatts of behind-the-meter dedicated capacity to its data center. It is a contracted, long-dated outlet outside fuel markets, but it is a single project still to be built, so we treat it as optionality rather than a driver of the next two years.

Chevron signed heads of agreements with the Government of Iraq to advance potential participation in the West Qurna 2 and Nasiriyah oilfield developments and an export pipeline. These are preliminary agreements, not reserves; turning them into production is uncertain and years away, so they carry no weight in our scenarios.

management.leadership: The 2026 proxy statement, filed April 7, 2026, lists the 2025 named executive officers as Michael K. Wirth, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer; Eimear P. Bonner, Chief Financial Officer; Mark A. Nelson, Vice Chairman; R. Hewitt Pate, Chief Legal Officer; and R. Clay Neff, President, Upstream, a new named executive officer for 2025. The board approved changes to certain officer titles on December 3, 2025. The stated objective is to safely deliver higher returns, lower carbon and superior shareholder value in any business environment. The recent record supports the execution claim: the Hess synergy and structural cost targets were both met early. In the Q2'26 release Wirth credited disciplined investment and strong execution for the quarter. Execution is not the issue in our call; the price is.
management.capitalAllocation: The proxy frames the policy as generating surplus cash flow in upside oil-price environments and securing the dividend and a strong balance sheet in downside environments. The second quarter fits that frame: with cash flow high, the company paid down debt while declaring its quarterly dividend. The board declared a $1.78 quarterly dividend in the July 31, 2026 release, payable September 10, 2026. The company also expects $1-2 billion a year of asset-sale proceeds through 2030. FY25 is the caution: returns exceeded free cash flow, as the cash-flow discussion shows, so the buyback is the flexible item if prices fall, while the proxy names securing the dividend and a strong balance sheet as the aims in downside environments. We read the allocation as disciplined, with the buyback pace as the variable to track.
management.governance: The 2026 proxy statement reports that every director who served in 2025, and Mr. Horton, is independent under NYSE standards, except Messrs. Hess and Wirth. The board has four standing committees: Audit; Board Nominating and Governance; Management Compensation; and Public Policy and Sustainability. The annual incentive plan weights financial results (35%), capital and cost management (30%), operating and safety performance (25%) and lower carbon (10%), capped at 200% of target. Long-term awards are half performance shares, with restricted stock units and stock options splitting the rest equally; the performance shares are judged 70% on relative total stockholder return and the remainder on relative ROCE improvement. The Governance Committee reviews related-person transactions under written guidelines. The structure is conventional for a company of this size and ties pay to returns and capital discipline.
management.insiderOwnership: As of March 16, 2026, the proxy counts 1,992,285,560 shares outstanding. The holders of more than 5% listed are The Vanguard Group at 8.56%, State Street Corporation at 7.50%, BlackRock, Inc. at 7.00% and Berkshire Hathaway Inc./Warren E. Buffett at 6.70%. The Vanguard figure is stale: it rests on a Schedule 13G/A filed February 13, 2024, and Vanguard later reported that certain of its subsidiaries or business divisions will report beneficial ownership separately. No single holder approaches control. All current non-employee directors and executive officers as a group held 11,240,082 shares, less than 1% of the class; Michael K. Wirth held 1,312,423 including stock units, and director John B. Hess held 8,798,589. For outside holders, alignment comes through the equity-heavy pay design rather than large insider stakes.

idiosyncratic: Commodity dependence: Chevron states that the price of crude oil is the most significant factor in upstream results. Q2'26 Brent averaged $104 against $68 a year earlier, and much of the year-over-year earnings gain would reverse if prices returned to that level, which is our Bear case.

Earnings beyond FY27: consensus already has EPS stepping down from FY26E to FY27E, and a further step down toward FY23–FY25 levels would cut the earnings our Base relies on, as the valuation section discusses.

Middle East conflict: it curtailed international production in the Partitioned Zone between Saudi Arabia and Kuwait, and supply disruptions cut international refinery crude inputs by 10 percent year over year in Q2'26; with lower gasoline and diesel demand, they also cut refined product sales by 13 percent. The risk factors also cite geopolitical tensions in Venezuela.

Leverage and returns: the FY25 debt increase and returns above free cash flow leave less room if prices fall before more debt is repaid; a downturn could force a choice between the buyback and the balance sheet.

Divestments: asset sales such as the Singapore Refining Company stake can produce gains or losses, and the company warns that decommissioning obligations transferred with sold assets have returned and may continue to return to it.
risks.systemic: Chevron's earnings are tied to the global economic cycle through commodity demand. Low or negative growth cuts demand for crude and refined products, and production quotas or other actions by OPEC or other producers can move prices regardless of Chevron's operations. The company warns that sustained lower prices could lead to asset impairments and cuts to capital spending, and that a sustained decline in liquidity could affect its credit ratings and potentially increase financing costs. Over a longer horizon the energy transition is the main systemic risk: policy, technology and changing consumer preferences could reduce demand for its core products. Physical risks from hurricanes, severe weather and wildfires, and cyber threats to operational technology networks, complete the exposures the filing highlights. None of these is specific to the current quarter, but each would bear on the Bear case.

body: We rate Chevron HOLD with a $182–$225 target range. The business is executing well: the Hess synergy and cost targets were met early, production and U.S. refinery throughput rose, and the second quarter brought a large debt paydown. But the shares trade near their 52-week high on earnings that consensus expects to fall, and our probability-weighted fair value of $200.50 sits slightly below the price. The dividend pays holders to wait; it does not make the shares cheap.

With the scenario prices held at their published dollar values, the math derives BUY only at or below our target low and SELL modestly above today's price, a level the shares exceeded on the way to the $217.78 52-week high. We would move to SELL if consensus earnings beyond FY27 fall clearly below FY27E, because that removes the support for our Base. We would move toward BUY if oil prices ease without the year-ahead EPS falling, which would show that Hess volumes and the structural savings have lifted the earnings base.
